title: Your own lament
hookLine: write a lament the way the psalmists did
last: IN WITH PAIN, OUT WITH RELIEF.

lines: DAVID TEARS HIS CLOTHES AND WEEPS.
THEN HE PUTS IT INTO WORDS.
cards: A man comes to David with his clothes torn and earth on his head. He brings news from the battle. Saul, the king, is dead.
So is Jonathan, Saul's son, David's friend. David doesn't make a speech about God's plan. The text says he tears his clothes, mourns, weeps, and fasts until evening.
And then he does something else. He puts the grief into words. The Bible calls it a lamentation, and it's today's model.

teach.b: Four things in David's lament, and anyone can borrow them. First, it's specific. It names names: Saul and Jonathan.
It names the place: the mountains of Gilboa, where they fell. It doesn't melt grief into a general mood.
Second, it has a refrain. The lament keeps coming back to the same cry, in the King James words: "How are the mighty fallen!" A refrain gives grief somewhere to return when the other words run out.
In between, David asks that the news not be told in the enemy's towns, so no one there can rejoice over it.
Third, it says what was good. Of Jonathan, David says: "very pleasant hast thou been unto me: thy love to me was wonderful, passing the love of women." A lament doesn't only count the loss.
It holds up what was lost, and it honors Saul as well as Jonathan.
Fourth, it doesn't fix anything. No lesson is tacked on at the end.
The last line returns to the refrain: "How are the mighty fallen, and the weapons of war perished!" The grief is allowed to stay grief. A lament isn't a complaint letter and it isn't a eulogy.
It's grief with a shape, honest enough to name what hurts and loving enough to name what was good.

how: Jews and Christians pray and read the laments of the Bible, including David's lament for Saul and Jonathan and the psalms of complaint, and some write laments of their own in grief.

games.q: you're David. the man with torn clothes has told you Saul and Jonathan are dead. what do you do?
o: weep, fast, and then put the grief into words.
games.why: David tears his clothes, weeps and fasts until evening, then laments for both of them, Saul included.

practice: On paper or a phone note, write six lines about one loss or hard thing: name it, what was good, what's gone, what hurts now, what you'd ask for if you could, and one short refrain to come back to.
It doesn't have to be poetry, and it doesn't have to be addressed to anyone; if you pray, you can address it to God, the way the psalmists did.

wordCard.voice: Qinah, Hebrew for a lament, the shape David gave his grief for Saul and Jonathan: specific, honest, and unfixed. Today's word.

orig.note: Hebrew: a lament, a dirge for the dead. David laments 'with this lamentation' in 2 Samuel 1:17.

carryVoice: Your line: my lament. Six honest lines are yours to keep, shown to no one. Day seven hundred forty, done.
